title: 1 Kings 8:54–66
context: Solomon rises from his knees and blesses the assembly, praising the LORD for giving rest to Israel and for keeping every word of his promise through Moses. He prays that God will stay with Israel and incline their hearts to walk in his ways, that his supplications will remain before the LORD, and that all peoples may know that the LORD is God. He calls Israel to wholehearted obedience. The king and people offer an enormous number of peace offerings, which the text gives as twenty-two thousand cattle and one hundred twenty thousand sheep, and the middle of the court is consecrated because the bronze altar is too small. A feast lasting twice seven days follows, with people from the entrance of Hamath to the brook of Egypt. The parallel in 2 Chronicles 7:1–10 includes details not found here and helps readers relate the fourteen days in 8:65 to the sending away of the people in 8:66.

verses.text: It was so, that when Solomon had finished praying all this prayer and supplication to the LORD, he arose from before the LORD’s altar, from kneeling on his knees with his hands spread out toward heaven.
verses.arminianNotes: The prayer over, the king gets up from the altar, where he had been kneeling. Arminian readers observe that the most powerful man in Israel prayed on his knees, a humble posture that models dependence on God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the king’s posture as acknowledging that his throne is under God’s rule. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as marking the end of the prayer, with 2 Chronicles 6:13 by reference adding detail about the setting.

verses.text: He stood and blessed all the assembly of Israel with a loud voice, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon stands and blesses the assembly with a loud voice. Arminian readers note the public nature of the blessing, as the king turns from speaking to God to speaking for God’s blessing over the people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the blessing as directing the people’s attention back to the LORD as the source of all good. Both traditions read the verse as a transition from prayer to praise and exhortation addressed to the assembly.

verses.text: “Blessed be the LORD, who has given rest to his people Israel, according to all that he promised. There has not failed one word of all his good promise, which he promised by Moses his servant.
verses.arminianNotes: Blessed be the LORD, who has given rest to Israel; not one word of his good promise through Moses has failed. Arminian readers see God’s faithfulness confirmed, echoing Joshua 21:45 and 23:14 by reference.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the fulfillment of every promise as testimony to God’s unfailing purpose. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as praise for God’s complete faithfulness, with rest in the land as the fruit of his promise (compare Deuteronomy 12:9–10).

verses.text: May the LORD our God be with us as he was with our fathers. Let him not leave us or forsake us,
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon prays that the LORD will be with Israel and not leave or forsake them. Arminian readers see a prayer for God’s continued presence, echoing promises such as Deuteronomy 31:6 and Joshua 1:5 by reference.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the prayer as resting on God’s faithfulness to his people. Shared ground: both traditions read the request as a heartfelt plea; on whether God’s people stay faithful to the end, see the existing contrast at 1 Samuel 12:22.

verses.text: that he may incline our hearts to him, to walk in all his ways, and to keep his commandments, his statutes, and his ordinances, which he commanded our fathers.
verses.arminianNotes: The purpose is that God may incline their hearts to walk in his ways. Arminian readers see grace that enables and draws the heart while leaving room for response; see the existing contrasts at Psalm 119:36 and Joshua 24:15.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a prayer that God will effectively turn the heart toward obedience, compare Deuteronomy 10:16 and 30:6. Shared ground: both traditions agree that obedience depends on God’s grace; their difference is already set out in those boxes.

verses.text: Let these my words, with which I have made supplication before the LORD, be near to the LORD our God day and night, that he may maintain the cause of his servant and the cause of his people Israel, as every day requires;
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon asks that his words remain before the LORD day and night, so that he maintains the cause of king and people as each day requires. Arminian readers see a desire for ongoing, daily dependence on God’s help.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the request as trusting God’s providence for daily needs, compare Matthew 6:11 by reference. Both traditions read the verse as joining a single prayer to the continuing life of Israel, day by day.

verses.text: that all the peoples of the earth may know that the LORD himself is God. There is no one else.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon looks for every people on earth to recognize that the LORD alone is God. Arminian readers hear a missionary note: Israel’s preservation is meant to bear witness far beyond its own borders.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the confession of the LORD’s uniqueness as the ultimate aim of the temple and its prayers. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as echoing Deuteronomy 4:35, with the nations’ knowledge of God as the goal.

verses.text: “Let your heart therefore be perfect with the LORD our God, to walk in his statutes, and to keep his commandments, as it is today.”
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon calls Israel to let their hearts be perfect with the LORD. Arminian readers see a real call to wholehearted obedience, and note that Solomon’s own heart is later said not to be perfect with the LORD (11:4).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the exhortation as following the prayer of 8:58: God’s grace and the call to obedience belong together. Both traditions read the verse as a sobering challenge, especially in light of the king’s own later failure.

verses.text: The king, and all Israel with him, offered sacrifice before the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The king and all Israel offer sacrifice before the LORD. Arminian readers see the whole community joining in worship, responding together to God’s faithfulness and presence in the new house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the sacrifices as fitting thanksgiving within the covenant order God established. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as introducing the great dedication offerings, made by king and people together.

verses.text: Solomon offered for the sacrifice of peace offerings, which he offered to the LORD, twenty two thousand head of cattle and one hundred twenty thousand sheep. So the king and all the children of Israel dedicated the LORD’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon offers twenty-two thousand cattle and one hundred twenty thousand sheep as peace offerings, and Israel dedicates the house. Arminian readers note the vast scale as the text gives it, showing extraordinary celebration.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the abundance as gratitude matching the greatness of the occasion. Both traditions state the numbers as the text gives them, noting that 2 Chronicles 7:5 gives the same figures by reference, and avoid speculating about them.

verses.text: The same day the king made the middle of the court holy that was before the LORD’s house; for there he offered the burnt offering, the meal offering, and the fat of the peace offerings, because the bronze altar that was before the LORD was too little to receive the burnt offering, the meal offering, and the fat of the peace offerings.
verses.arminianNotes: The king consecrates the middle of the court because the bronze altar is too small for the offerings. Arminian readers note the practical response to the scale of worship, making room for all that was offered.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the consecration as done before the LORD, showing that even necessary adjustments are made within the order of worship. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a practical detail highlighting the size of the celebration.

verses.text: So Solomon held the feast at that time, and all Israel with him, a great assembly, from the entrance of Hamath to the brook of Egypt, before the LORD our God, seven days and seven more days, even fourteen days.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon holds the feast with a great assembly from the entrance of Hamath to the brook of Egypt, for fourteen days. Arminian readers note the wide reach of the gathering, representing the land’s northern and southern limits.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the assembly as a picture of a united people rejoicing before God. Both traditions acknowledge that the exact locations of the entrance of Hamath and the brook of Egypt are debated, and that 2 Chronicles 7:8–10 helps explain the fourteen days.

verses.text: On the eighth day he sent the people away; and they blessed the king, and went to their tents joyful and glad in their hearts for all the goodness that the LORD had shown to David his servant, and to Israel his people.
verses.arminianNotes: On the eighth day the people go home joyful for all the goodness the LORD showed to David and Israel. Arminian readers see joy as the fitting result of experiencing God’s faithfulness together.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the people’s gladness as rooted in God’s goodness to David, the covenant king. Shared ground: both traditions read the ending as a high point of Israel’s history, though later chapters show how quickly faithfulness would falter.
